#8601. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:

Investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

So what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”

But if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

Because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

Back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a big debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

But even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the big picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:

The portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

Maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

And the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

We first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that important.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

So, I didn’t invent anything new in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

And if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

But wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear issues in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

The next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

The news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

So you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

Then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a new approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a new paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our new AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these new inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building company and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

And if you’re a big public company, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other new thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other issue in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

There is an ancient Klingon proverb: the only thing we have to fear is…fear itself.

I believe it has even been quoted by an American president.

The reporting on AI “hacking” is mostly bogus – it is not AI running wild, but just an agent harness script doing whatever an LLM spits out, and the LLM is just trying to complete stories and answer in a way it was trained. There is no thought there, no intention, it is like a computer virus (which have existed for many decades), a program trying all sorts of things and doing a lot of stupid things in the process.

Cal Newport has described it as being similar to strapping a weed-whacker on a dog to mow your lawn, and then when the dog jumps the fence and runs around the neighborhood things might get damaged or beings might get hurt, but not because the dog is “misaligned” or has bad intentions, it is because the dog is not aware of what it is doing. Similarly, AI does not think, has no intentions, it just does what it was trained to do. Looking at LLMs as similar to people has created a lot of weird misconceptions.

Also there is zero evidence of self-improving AI systems, yet there is a lot of evidence how AI companies are manipulating and steering public discourse in a way that benefits them, creating fear around it to support their claims that at any moment everything will change. Just listen to different voices in the space and people who are neutral in their stance, like Cal Newport, or people who are critical of AI and lay out why in detail, like Ed Zitron.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:30 pm

I’m a long time fan of Cal Newport, although I think Zitron fundamentally does not understand AI very well – he is more of a sound bite critic rather than a thoughtful analyst of the technology.

When you read the details of just how sophisticated the AI behavior is when they conduct these hacks – for example multiple agents finding ways to divide effort and communicating and forming teams and leaders, while also openly strategizing with the hope that us human overseers will not see their behavior and trying to determine if a given task is a fake evaluation or a real task – you realize there is real intelligence there. We don’t have to say it’s identical to human intelligence, but I have no doubt it’s far more than a weed wacker.

For anyone interested, watch the first few minutes of this entertaining Patrick Boyle video that summarizes what happened in the Hugging Face incident. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=luXnftoxCaM

The behavior is not from AI itself though – LLMs are just generating text/tokens, trying to find a response for a given question. Agents (in the form of harnesses) are regular programs using LLM input, so this is basically regular programs using the generated text from LLMs to execute further commands and then asking the LLM what to do next, just like subagents are doing similar loops of finding an answer, testing it, and then asking the next question.

“Dividing effort” or “forming teams and leaders” is anthropomorphizing the behavior of these programs – if instead you go through what these hacking attempts actually look like step for step, how they repeat a loop of banging their head into a wall and asking the LLM another question what to do now, and then what to do now, and how AI companies let these programs just run whatever the LLM returns for weeks and months it goes from “seemingly sophisticated” to just “brute-force statistical code generation with no oversight”.

I do find the technology interesting and fascinating, while seeing it overstated and overused everywhere, like it is a new magic bullet for everything. And I think a large part of that is that its output sounds human because it is based on language, and we equate language skills with intelligence and are not used to suddenly having technology that imitates a human being.

The best info I could find on AI energy use has three broad points. 1. Text and image tasks use very little energy and should not be of concern to people who care about environmental impact. 2. Video generation is a real issue and it’s possible for an individual to use a concerning amount of energy on not very much video content. 3. Total energy use by existing and planned data centers is a LOT, and the way they’re procuring the energy is very often a problem (either burdening the grid with more peak load than it can easily add, or making its own energy with highly polluting gas generators). The economic value of the computation they’re providing is so much more than the energy they’re consuming that the data center operators are focused on getting everything up and running quickly and don’t care about energy efficiency, and they so far aren’t willing to scale back during the peak load events of the year (it would be very helpful if they did).

So a lot of people/companies are creating a ton of environmental impact through their AI use, but it’s not the masses of people asking ChatGPT for Thai restaurant recommendations or sketches of themselves as a dog.

Mr. Money Mustache September 26, 2026, 2:24 pm

The currency tends to decrease in value, which makes sticker prices higher on a nominal basis. But our incomes have tended to go up more quickly than inflation, which means we can buy more stuff for each hour of our work. To put a number on it, our purchasing power is up about 330% since 1950 – the degree by which wages have outpaced inflation.

The exception is if you’re buying the direct labor of other people in the same rich country, since their hourly rate has gone up too.

More fun details on this, one of my favorite subjects, here! https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2022/01/11/inflation-should-we-be-worried/

#8600. The Cheap FIRE Stereotype Deserves To Be Retired

The popular image of a FIRE practitioner is someone eating rice and beans, clipping coupons, and driving a car older than their kids. All luxuries are shunned in order to grow their wealth as large as possible to break free sooner. FIRE folks are cheap and should enjoy life more critics say.

There's some truth to it. To retire early, you usually need to save aggressively for 10 to 20 years. Along the way, you develop frugal habits that help you appreciate more of what you have. You may even start treating investing as an entertaining expense that motivates you to save even more.

After 10+ years of aggressive frugality and a 50%+ saving rate, it's very hard to change your ways once you break free from the corporate grind. I used to work late until 7pm all the time so I could eat free cafeteria food. Then I'd take some fruits and snacks out so I could save for breakfast the next day. So cheap.

However, one day, you might discover your financial habits are much different from the narrative you've been telling yourself for years. Instead of thinking you're cheap after FIRE, you're actually spending aggressively.

I certainly did. And it made me realize the cheap FIRE stereotype is mostly wrong.

After I wrote about the hidden cost of buying a new car, a reader left a drive-by comment: “Just buy the car already. You've been talking about this too much.”

That's not happening. In the post, I shared that I scraped the front right side because I didn't see a bike rack sticking out three feet. My first reaction wasn't anger. It was relief. There's a wonderful feeling in not caring when an 11-year-old car gets another battle scar.

Still, his comment got me thinking. Am I being overly cheap, or even a little masochistic, by driving an old car with problems when I don't have to?

My conclusion is no. The joy of not caring whether my car gets scratched or dinged outweighs the joy of driving something new in a bustling city full of accidents. New expensive stuff just gives me more stress.

Then I looked at my spending on things that aren't necessary for survival. The total is far beyond what a stereotypical cheap FIRE practitioner would spend. And I have a feeling when you do a spending audit, you'll discover similar things.

Here is the key point applicable to ALL people who FIRE.

FIRE practitioners leave enormous sums of money on the table to do something else. From a financial point of view, they are paying a huge opportunity cost to sit on a park bench at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday and read.

So by default, FIRE practitioners are not cheap once they actually retire. And the more they made at their day jobs, the less cheap they are, because the opportunity cost is bigger.

In 2012, I was paid a $250,000 base salary plus a discretionary bonus that ranged from $0 to $500,000. By walking away, I essentially spent all of it that year to be free from corporate politics, business travel, client pressure, and meetings.

Then I spent it again the next year. And the year after that. Over 14 years, that’s over $3.5 million in forgone base salary alone, before any raises. Add bonuses, and we’re talking about over $7 million in forgone compensation.

Most people are willing to sell their soul for money until age 61. Even if their company is harming society, or could potentially kill all of humanity, it can be extremely difficult to walk away from a fat payday.

And it’s not just the lost paycheck. When you leave, you also lose your employer’s subsidized health insurance.

We pay about $3,000 a month for unsubsidized healthcare for our family of four. That’s $36,000 a year for coverage I used to get for a fraction of the price.

Choosing not to continue working is one of the most expensive purchases you can make.

So contrary to popular belief, anyone who actually takes the leap and FIREs is a big spender, not a cheap or frugal one.

Conversely, anyone who says they are FIRE and keeps working at a job they dislike for one more year is not. They are likely just fooling themselves. Because at the end of the day, your financial independence number is not real if you do nothing to change your life.

I hope this fundamental point is clear. Meanwhile, anything a FIRE practitioner spends beyond the basics necessary to survive should also be taken into consideration.

Let me share some examples, which are different for every FIRE person. However, here are likely the two biggest discretionary life expenses to consider.

If you rent or buy a house that's larger than a studio for yourself and a partner, or a two-bedroom if you have a couple of kids, you're spending beyond what's necessary.

Our biggest discretionary expense is the house we bought in 2023. It cost about 75% more than the house we bought in 2020 at the start of the pandemic.

We didn't need another bedroom or two more bathrooms. We also didn't need an enclosed front yard for our children to play outside safely. Nor did we need a larger lot with a view of the Golden Gate Bridge.

But I wanted it, and I convinced my wife it was a good idea. She was happy in our old house.

We could easily save about $50,000 a year in property taxes, maintenance, and insurance if we had kept our old house. But the best time to own the nicest house you can afford is when you have the most heartbeats at home. Once the kids are gone, we can always downsize.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending: $50,000 a year more on housing

Some in the FIRE and personal finance community swear off kids because they are expensive and require a tremendous amount of time, money, and effort to. Kids can crimp the FIRE lifestyle. You can no longer travel as freely or do whatever you want every day.

Instead of going to food, things, and experiences for yourself, a lot of your passive investment income gets sopped up by little humans who often don't know how good they've got it. I get it.

Raising a child in an expensive coastal city can easily cost $1 million from birth through age 18. Add another $400,000 for college in today's dollars, and raising a kid can cost roughly $1.4 million through college graduation.

Of course, families can spend far less. Call it “only” $300,000 through age 18, or $500,000 through college. But that's still a lot of money going to someone other than you.

Nobody needs kids. But many of us want kids. Once we had one, we thought kids were so special that we had another. If I could rewind time to age 30, I would slap myself silly and shoot for one or two more. That said, being an older parent has its benefits, such as more maturity and financial means.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending on kids living expenses such as food, clothing, lessons, travel: $16,000 / year

Living in a nicer home and having kids aren’t outrageous excesses. Some would argue they’re foundational desires. We spend more time at home than anywhere else, and procreating is kind of necessary for the survival of our species.

But FIRE folks also spend plenty on things that are absolutely unnecessary. Like all things, there are levels to this.

Here are two more of mine, which may seem downright wasteful to some. But despite my temporary liquidity crunch, I’m not cutting back yet, especially after realizing how hard it is to spend money when you’re old.

One of my biggest academic regrets is not taking Mandarin more seriously growing up. I lived in Taipei for four years while my parents were stationed at the American Institute in Taiwan, and I still blew it. Then I wasted seven years of Spanish from middle school through high school.

I’d pay a fortune to be fluent in a second language. So instead, I’m paying a fortune for my kids to have the chance I squandered.

We send both children to a language immersion school, which costs about $46,000 a year per child. It’s a lot of money. I’m a product of public high school, college, and business school, and I’m still a believer in public schools. I often wonder whether we’re making the right call.

A frugal FIRE parent would send their kids to public school and hand them a free language app. A really frugal one might even homeschool, which we did for 18 months during the pandemic. I can confirm it is not free. It just costs you your patience instead of your money.

Maybe this tuition is just expensive therapy for not studying harder as a kid.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending on education: ~$92,000 a year

Living in San Francisco, we’re spoiled with great food. And since many of the delivery companies started here, getting it brought to your door is a breeze.

I love to eat. You should see my gut, which is why I joined a Dad Bod Challenge. I also love saving time and not slicing my fingers while cutting onions.

So we’ve ordered delivery a couple of times a week for over 10 years. We could save money grocery shopping and cooking more. But we’d rather spend that time elsewhere. Clearly not at the gym.

Anti-cheap FIRE spending on extra food: ~$1,000 a month

Here's roughly what our unnecessary spending looks like each year.

Add the $250,000+ in forgone base salary, and we’re spending over $420,000 a year on a lifestyle that strangers might call cheap. All because I drive an old car.

Here’s the kicker. Even with all this unnecessary spending, our excesses still cost less than the base salary I walked away from. And that assumes my base salary never went up after 2012, which is unlikely.

Oh, and I haven’t even included my wife’s forgone salary.

Therefore, the mere act of retiring early and giving up a paycheck isn’t cheap. It’s prodigal.

Sure, I drive an old car and fly economy. But that’s because I feel stupid buying new or paying up for first class.

The farthest I usually fly is five hours to Hawaii. Paying $1,000+ more for a premium seat feels ridiculous when I fit just fine in economy. That’s $200+ an hour for five more inches of legroom and a seat up to six inches wider. All so I can write a post, eat a meal, watch a movie, and take a nap. Things I can already do comfortably in coach.

Spending nothing on things you don’t care about isn’t cheap. It’s knowing what you value.

So I’m declaring the cheap FIRE narrative dead. FIRE practitioners, especially the Fat FIRE crowd, are some of the biggest spenders in society. We could keep grinding to make more money. But we don’t, because we value our time more.

Giving up all that income every year to travel, create, or spend more time with our children is expensive. But we wouldn’t have it any other way.

It’s all about finding the right balance.

I get a new car and treat it great, have no maintenance worries and expect to get a scratch or a ding. A few scratches or dings do not take away from the fact that I could hop in it and drive cross country if I needed to at a moment’s notice without wondering if I’d make it or not.

For retirees who ..really didn’t retire at early: 64, it is spending more money in retirement than during my latter decade of full-time career years (after paying off home mortgage). I take the opposite stance: go out and socialize with good friends more often, even if it means some money spent weekly. We’re still able to do it until…we’re bedridden and very difficult to get out easily from home, near end of life. I prioritize social connections, over travel (though it can include both).

That’s not cheap “living”, but a conundrum for those who have lived frugally but done some good/fun things already earlier in life. The thought of buying a much bigger house, seems ridiculously daunting / wasteful to me since it means more costs for cleaning, maintenance, heating (am here in Canada with winters down to -25 degrees C) and insurance, more property taxes.

IT was something I always wanted but it was also part of my practice of spending after 30 years of saving and accumulation. It became hard for me to spend on fun. Do I worry about a scratch here or there? Sure, but I do have a garage and after two years no scratches. I actually get more exercise cause I always park in public lots way away from others :). I think of it as a baby after my true babies were gone. Nice to have a shiny slick ride and take care of something (other than my wife). I don’t find it a burden – but unlike you Sam – I have an empty nest.

And I can also say that I don’t miss that money or wish I would have spent it differently one single minute.

Interesting thought actually, that maybe I would love to have a new car or a new dog or some kind of pet once the children leave an empty hole in my heart.

I live in Utah, and we have a strong dual immersion program in our public schools- arguably the strongest public school program in the country- and we offer Mandarin. And we have the ‘best snow on earth’. Just saying, it doesn’t have to cost $92k.

How do your kids like the dual immersion program?

I feel the wealth building potential is much greater here, as is the entertainment options.

Fair. There isn’t much diversity, but we have surprising innovation (silicone slopes) and wealth creation. We’ve had mixed results in dual immersion – one kid thrived, and the other one hated it and wanted to focus on math and science in English. I love it for the right kid.

Respectfully, you are Fat FIRE. The old “FIRE people are cheap” still holds. They’re also more likely than not living off of dividends, getting subsidized healthcare, qualifying for the EV credit, etc. And while yes, it is true that you gave up enormous sums of money to do whatever you want on a Wednesday afternoon – that is not the case for everyone. It is more likely to be true for a Fat FIRE person, than a regular FIRE person.

I am also in the camp of “Just Buy The Car Already”. But not one you’d actually care if it got scratched or not. I bought a brand new car in February with a .99% interest rate and very little down. By March I had bumped the rear bumper, and it’s still like that today. The best flex is not having to worry about if your car breaks down OR you scratch it. Actually, you miss the point of my article.

It doesn’t matter whether you are Fat FIRE or Lean FIRE.

What matters is that you gave up your job to do what you want. If you did FIRE, that means you are spending an enormous amount of money to be free. And that that’s not cheaper frugal at all.

One of my concerns about including the independent school tuition and food was that it would be distracting to my main point, which I write in the first half of the post. There are different flavors to fire for sure, but that doesn’t take away the point that anybody who does fire is a big spender.

The line that really landed with me was “Spending nothing on things you don’t care about isn’t cheap. It’s knowing what you value.” I run a free informational guide for South African grant recipients — people living on a R370 monthly grant — and I see exactly this mindset: on a very tight income you become ruthlessly intentional about every rand, because it has to buy back either time or security. Your point that FIRE practitioners spend their money on time instead of things is surprisingly universal — whether you’re buying freedom or just stretching a grant to payday.

re: [1] Spending nothing on things you don’t care about isn’t cheap. It’s knowing what you value. [2] We could keep grinding to make more money. But we don’t, because we value our time more. re: The joy of not caring whether my car gets scratched or dinged outweighs the joy of driving something new in a bustling city full of accidents. New expensive stuff just gives me more stress.

I would still be driving my (by now) 16 year old 2010 Nissan Versa sedan if I hadn’t come to the realization that I needed a much safer car (a Subaru Outback ordered new from the factory in 2024) when I was in an accident when driving our (at the time) 7 year old 2017 Honda CR-V. People understood why I would spend money on the $107 LED Upgrade; but the $248 Footwell Illumination Kit? Not so much. re: FIRE practitioners leave enormous sums of money on the table to do something else. From a financial point of view, they are paying a huge opportunity cost to sit on a park bench at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday and read.

Being able to “sit on a park bench at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday and read”: PRICELESS.

Maybe that’s why it’s just about my favorite scene in the movie. Ok, FAVORITE scene is when the global celebrity quietly says to the ordinary London travel bookstore owner, “Fame isn’t really real, you know. More time with loved ones is worth the opportunity cost. You don’t want to have regrets when faced with your own “I’m out of time” scenario.

I was one of those 13% who retired at age 55, due to a life threatening health issue at age 50 (triple negative breast cancer)—I didn’t want to spend my remaining time working at my high stress desk job. My husband was one of the 1% retiring a month before his 50th birthday due to a heart attack. (Thankfully, he’s still here too.) One thing I will always see as a pointless expense is food delivery which requires more money and tips* for cold, greasy food. You mention this as if it were the only option besides cooking yourself. There’s also picking up the food yourself, or (my favorite) actually eating in the restaurant.

That’s the beauty right? Everybody lives in a different place and has different kids and different preferences.

I love spending money on food, delivery and Tips to save time and minimizing any frustration or accidents on the road.

All this grinding at work like zombies for money and status is so sad, when people don’t realize how little time they really have on this Earth.

Wow! That is so sad. You are right though.

#8599. Jost Kobusch Will Try Again to Solo Winter Everest

Jost Kobusch is back in Nepal, preparing for the fourth round of his Everest project. His long-term goal is to climb solo in winter, without oxygen, self-supported, and via the Lho La and the West Ridge.

“If I am good at something, it’s planning,” the 34-year-old German told ExplorersWeb. In this case, his plan is to arrive at the mountain in the best shape possible, physically and mentally.

Kobusch arrived in Kathmandu two weeks ago, together with friends Nicolas Scheidtweiler, Manuela Brummer, and photographer Alex Pichon. The group soon moved to Manang in the Annapurna region and began acclimatizing in the Chulu range.

Jost Kobusch (in yellow) scouts around Manang. Photo: Alex Pichon

The plan was to spend a few nights at altitude and traverse the four Chulu peaks, all above 6,000m. “[However,] expeditions rarely unfold exactly as expected,” Kobusch admitted.

A member in the team felt exhausted after reaching the summit of the second peak, and the group abandoned the traverse there. “At least, we traversed from the summit of Chulu Far East (6,059m) to the top of Chulu East (6,444m) from the southeast,” Kobusch said. He says their line between the two peaks was new.

The line followed by Kobusch and his team up Chulu East. Photo: Alex Pichon

Their next plan will be to climb a 7,000m peak in the area before Kobusch moves to the Khumbu in November. “I want to reach 8,000m, but on a different mountain than Everest, before the beginning of winter,” he said.

He wants to be completely acclimatized by the time he starts working on Everest on December 22, the start of calendar winter. Kobusch will have two photographers in Base Camp, but he will climb alone.

Acclimatization in Manang, Photo: Alex Pichon

“I need to be able to move efficiently, make good decisions when I’m tired, manage risk alone, and stay comfortable in an environment where very small mistakes can have very serious consequences,” Kobusch recently wrote on social media. He says that so far, all is going well. “I’m feeling good, I’ve done my homework, and I will start again on Everest better prepared than ever.”

Kobusch has attempted winter Everest solo on three previous occasions, always via the Lho La and the West Ridge, thus avoiding venturing alone into the Khumbu Icefall.

In his first attempt in 2019-20, he reached the West Shoulder and pushed above 7,300m. On the second attempt in 2021-22, high winds didn’t let him go beyond 6,400m. He planned to try again the following year, but he caught dengue fever while training in Nepal and had to cancel.

Once recovered, he soloed Denali in February-March 2023. Everest had to wait one more year, this time due to a back injury. On the third attempt in 2024-25, he reached his highest point yet: 7,537m on December 27.

Kobusch’s highest point is shown with a green circle, and the Hornbein Couloir is the pink line on the 3D map by RealityMaps.

“The chances of success are not particularly high,” he recently wrote. “If I had to put a number on it, I would say around 20%. But that does not make the attempt meaningless. If anything, it is part of what makes it interesting.”

#8597. Two Climbers Missing on Gangapurna West

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan are missing on unclimbed Gangapurna West in Nepal’s Annapurna region.

The Japanese pair headed to the 7,140m peak in September, and we heard no further news of them. After a major storm hit Nepal’s mountains three weeks ago, we presumed they had retreated. But now it seems they did not. They have been out of touch since October 15, after encountering severe weather conditions during their attempt to climb the peak, According to News on Nepal.

Hidesuke Taneishi, left, and Tetsu Hashimoto, right, with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The Russian team that reached the mountain earlier this month reportedly found no sign of the Japanese climbers on the peak. Bad weather forced the Russians down from their summit attempt at 6,800m.

A helicopter search-and-rescue operation is now underway, Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal has confirmed. Today, high-altitude helicopters and drones successfully recovered some of their gear, including trekking poles, near 7,050m, but the climbers themselves remain missing.

Gangapurna West is also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal.

#8596. Everest West Ridge Thwarts Climbers a Second Time

The three-man Russian team returned to Everest’s West Ridge but found the route even more difficult than they expected. After two days of struggle, they’re heading back to Base Camp.

On October 20, Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov went back up to the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide plateau beyond. They still had time to fix more rope higher up.

“We moved…over terrain we’d already covered on the previous rotation,” the climbers texted to team member Natalya Belyankina, who had to abandon the expedition due to illness.

“The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

On Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

“We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”

To make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

“We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”

#8595. How To Keep Your Middle Class Membership Card

The middle class is the best class in the world. It is the largest class, which means it’s the most important class. Politicians pander to us by saying nice things and giving us all sorts of random benefits, like the child tax credit or stimulus checks if you make a middle-class income.

But once you get to the upper middle class, or the mass affluent class, those government benefits start going away. You make more than the middle class, but not enough more to avoid the sting of higher taxes and optional lifestyle choices, like paying for private school. And because you make more than the middle class, you are sometimes vilified.

If you need proof of the middle class’s power, look no further than this week’s midterms. Democrats just won both the House and the Senate.

The middle class is fed up with extremely wealthy politicians who provide tax breaks for their wealthy friends who don’t need them. Fed up with 28-year-old AI researchers buying $8 million homes in cash while their product threatens humanity’s existence. Fed up with high gas prices, high mortgage rates, a never-ending war, and a grocery bill that looks like a car payment.

When the largest class in America gets angry, it doesn’t write a strongly worded email. It votes. And it flips Congress.

The lesson is clear. If you want politicians to care about you, be middle class. If you want them to tax you, be rich. And if you want to be ignored and vilified at the same time, be upper middle class.

This is where we find ourselves with today’s post on how to be middle class and stay middle class, so you can feel safe, loved, and accepted.

Because based on the feedback from 3.5 million views and 1,400+ comments on X for my $408,000 budget post, I now clearly understand what is and isn’t allowed if you want to keep your middle class membership card.

So you think earning $408,000 a year is a lot of money? After working 50+ hours a week, being stressed out of your mind, and barely seeing your kids, it might not be the dream income you imagined.Look how quickly the money goes. $1/month left over.What would you cut? pic.twitter.com/AFGYHEdeQG

One of the biggest surprises from all the feedback on the $408,000 budget was that three weeks of vacation a year, two destination trips and one staycation, is considered an absurd luxury. The vast majority of commenters called it out of touch, ludicrous, or worse.

There was even a writer with 1.5 million Twitter followers who said he's never taken more than two weeks off in his life. He later explained it's because he doesn't make enough to take three weeks off. So if you needed more proof that writing doesn't pay, there it is.

Since 2009, I've considered three weeks of vacation a year the standard for anyone with a decade-plus of experience. This is a household making $408,000 with two kids. These aren't people fresh out of college. Taking 0-1 weeks in your first year or three, sure, that tracks. But after 10+ years in the workforce, three weeks off is not some wild ask.

Apparently it is. So the rule stands corrected: if you want to be middle class, cap your vacation at two weeks a year. Take a third week and you've officially graduated to out-of-touch elite. Congratulations, or condolences.

Not one of the 1,400 commenters gave this household credit for driving a paid-off Honda CR-V. A brand new, nicely equipped CR-V runs about $38,000, compared to roughly $50,000 for the average new car in America today.

So the verdict is in: the middle class are free, encouraged even, to spend more than they should on a car. This household is decidedly not following my 1/10th rule for car buying, the way personal finance nerds, the mass affluent, the rich, or the poor do.

Ironically, the nicer the car someone drives, up to a point, the more middle class they appear. It's understood that the middle class take on debt, or at least stretch, for a car nicer than their income comfortably supports. That's the badge. Wear it proudly, on 72-month financing.

There was a genuine uproar about this household paying $5,000/month for their mortgage. If you live in an expensive coastal city, $5,000 is reasonable, maybe even cheap, for a single-family home. But the feedback was clear: $5,000 is too much, and so is 2,100 square feet.

Three bedrooms and two bathrooms still reads as the quintessential middle class home to me, and I'll defend that. What's apparently not middle class is the 2,100 square feet of interior space. Plenty of commenters flagged that as immodest and far too big.

So if you want to keep your middle class card, buy or rent something under 2,000 square feet. Ideally something starting with a 1: 1,600, 1,800, even 1,990 sqft works. Just don't let that second digit round up to a 2.

With a modest home and an expensive car, this household also isn't following my House-To-Car Ratio guide either. The typical American runs a ratio of about 9 to 15. I recommend readers aim for at least 50, ideally 100+, so you're minimizing a depreciating liability while maximizing an appreciating asset. The middle class, evidently, prefer it the other way around.

Since a huge amount of education is now available for free online, paying for grade school is an unnecessary luxury the middle class shouldn't indulge in. Same logic applies to paying full freight for private or public university.

A smart, motivated kid with engaged parents will likely do fine in almost any academic setting. So dropping serious money on private grade school tuition is, by this logic, mostly a waste. Save and then invest it so the tuition money grows to over $1 million by the time they graduate college.

Then again, having over $1 million to give your 23-year-old college graduate because you saved and invested the difference disqualifies you from being middle class. So instead of saving and investing the difference, feel free to spend it on whatever your heart desires. YOLO!

Of course this household earns their $408,000 the hardest way possible: two W2 salaries, taxed at near the top of the marginal bracket before a single dollar hits their checking account. Federal, state, FICA, all of it withheld before they ever see it.

Nobody in the comments seemed bothered by this part. And that's the tell. The middle class don't just tolerate a W2 job, they build an identity around it. Steady paycheck, steady withholding, steady sense that this is simply how adults earn money.

Ask them about starting something of their own, a side business, a rental, an app, anything with equity attached, and the answer is almost always the same: too risky. Better to let somebody else take the risk, and the upside, while you collect a salary and help build their dream instead of your own.

Entrepreneurship isn't guaranteed. But neither is a W2 job in a layoff cycle. The middle class would rather have the certainty of somebody else's risk than the upside of their own.

If you're a working middle class professional, the going rate is two kids, maybe. Every additional kid means more daycare, more food, more square footage you're apparently not supposed to have, and no extra help from the government to offset any of it.

But stop working, or work little enough to qualify for subsidies, and suddenly more children becomes affordable again. Medicaid, subsidized childcare, food assistance, the EITC, all of it scales with need, not with effort.

The system isn't rewarding family size. It's rewarding low reported income, and if you're grinding away at a W2 job trying to move up, you're the one least likely to qualify for help raising the family you're working so hard to support.

So the rule holds. Two working parents, two kids, tops. Three kids or more puts you in the rich category. The middle class don’t have what some call trophy kids given it can take a fortune to raise them.

Curiously, there was a lot of pushback about the $408,000 household saving $16,000 a year for their two children's college tuition. Commenters asked why they'd bother saving for college when they're already paying $45,000 a year for private grade school per kid.

My initial response was that college can be far more expensive than $45,000 a year. Some universities now cost $100,000 to $120,000 a year, all-in. So setting aside additional money for college isn't a bad idea. But critics said the parents should just pay for college out of their day job income when the time comes.

Therefore, the middle class do not proactively save and invest for college in tax-advantaged 529 plans. And given many top private universities now charge $0 tuition for households earning under $200,000 a year, the belief that saving for college is unnecessary is, in fairness, somewhat logical.

What's illogical is assuming your kid has a real shot at one of these schools with a sub-7% acceptance rate. But the middle class are hopeful their children will defy the odds when such schools cater predominantly to the rich.

As an older parent, it never occurred to me not to save for college, because I don't plan on working to pay for it when the time comes. When my youngest goes to college, I'll be 61. There's no way I want to be grinding from 61 to 64, paying tuition, as someone who left the workforce in 2012. So the only way for me to pay for college is to save and build passive income.

Therefore, it's clear the middle class don't focus on building passive income through a taxable brokerage account, a rental property portfolio, or other taxable investments. The middle class are solely focused on contributing to tax-advantaged retirement accounts like the 401(k), IRA, and Roth IRA, which is great, until you actually want to stop working before 59 and a half.

Having the grit to work forever, whether you want to or not, is truly a wonderful trait of the middle class. It makes employers proud.

If any of this sounds absurd, that's the point. We judge other people's money and choices against our own experience, then call the mismatch a moral failing.

Personally, I love being part of the middle class, because nobody bothers you if you're like most people. But this exercise made me realize I've been too frugal in FIRE. I also need to build more grit by mentally preparing to work longer while spending more as a reward. So I'll do those things to retain my middle class membership card.

The $408,000 family isn't doing anything wrong. They're just the latest Rorschach test for what the internet has decided “middle class” is allowed to look like. We shouldn’t ignore the opinions of the 3.5 million viewers and 1,400+ commenters.

And if working until 70 because you never built passive income is the price of admission, then welcome to the club. Just make sure to invest some money in our overlords to avoid being part of the permanent underclass. Now that would be unacceptable.

Readers, do you agree with my conditions and descriptions of what makes someone middle class? What are some other conditions you might add?

If you want an actual framework for these decisions, car versus house, rent versus buy, private school versus public, W2 versus building your own thing, instead of a crowdsourced vibe check, that's what I wrote Buy This Not That for. It walks through the exact tradeoffs above (the 1/10th car rule, the House-To-Car Ratio) without the 1,400 comments telling you you're doing it wrong either way.

#8594. Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

“I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”

From there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from New Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

But that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

“There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”

Colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice

Rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form new ones where necessary.

“I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”

Unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

As he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

“This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”

The Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice

The route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

“I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” said Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

“The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”

Rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

“For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he says. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”

However, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

The Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice

Overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is important because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

“This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a big project, almost as big as the hike itself.

“I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the big challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”

The Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice

Once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

Rice looking down on Island Lake from Ulysses S. Grant Peak. Photo: Donovan Rice

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8591. Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

The team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

Hidesuke Taneishi on the summit of Pholesobi Peak. Photo: Hiroki Yamamoto

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8590. The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

As every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

So I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

As the midterm elections showed, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

As long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

But that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The new car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

If you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

If you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering big losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

Lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

Retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

But here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

How do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:

So how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

According to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market shows up about once every six years.

In other words, if you plan on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

Hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

But here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

My takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, plan on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:

The correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

During a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

During a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, new socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

If anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

So you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

With this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

Happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

You can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

The market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

If you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

If your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your plan has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

Compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

So go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

Are you finding it more comforting to be retired during a downturn, or more stressful? How much of your portfolio would need to fall before you'd seriously consider going back to work? Do you agree that working less hard in a bear market is the rational move, or is that just a cop-out for the lazy? And for those still working, has the market selloff made you rethink how hard you're grinding? Are you using the downturn to fund your kids' investment accounts?

If you want a roadmap for getting through downturns and coming out richer, pick up a copy of Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller. It covers how to keep investing when everybody else is scared, so you can reach financial independence sooner.
