#8556. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8555. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8554. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8550. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8547. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8544. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

#8540. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

#8538. South Dakota Is Losing Its Hometown Pheasant Hunters. Meanwhile, the Nonresident Business Is Booming

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:52 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I was hunting a strip of public walk-in access across the road from a fleet of combines. As the harvesters crawled closer, pheasants kept flushing out of the standing corn and into the chest-high cover I was following my dog through. I marked one rooster that landed 300 yards ahead and, when Hatchet eventually trailed and flushed him, I was ready.

But I never shouldered my gun. The bird flushed straight toward the cab of a grain truck and veered out of range. The man sitting behind the windshield, who looked to be in his 20s, threw up his arms. Worried I might be irritating the farmers despite my restraint, I headed for my truck — the one with the Arkansas plates — with the birds I’d already killed. I know I’m a visitor here, and I don’t want to contribute to an existing problem.

This fall I drove 10 hours from my home to hunt public-land pheasants. It’s my seventh season in a row making the trip, and I can’t remember ever seeing more pickups loaded with kennels and coolers on I-29. We were all South Dakota bound.

As I’ve hunted my tried-and-true public spots and explored new ones this year, I’ve been surprised (though seldom hindered) by the number of fellow hunters getting after it. Each time I pass a truck parked in the ditch, I can’t help but clock the license plate: Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota. I’ve yet to spot a South Dakota plate that seems to belong to a pheasant hunter.

Anecdotal though it may be, my experience tracks with a broader trend in South Dakota. Annual harvest surveys show nonresident pheasant hunters are outnumbering resident hunters, and have every year since 2002. Last season approximately 57,100 residents hunted pheasants, while about 82,600 nonresidents hunted pheasants, according to those survey projections from South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks.

And during opening weekend on Oct. 17 and 18, SDGFP conservation officers talked with some 1,800 pheasant hunters. They hailed from 44 different states.

Many South Dakotans worry their home state is too busy courting these nonresident hunters — or more precisely, their wallets — to notice the fading tradition of resident pheasant culture.

“We love out-of-state hunters. And we want everybody to keep coming and enjoying South Dakota’s tradition,” says Brad Johnson, a South Dakota real-estate appraiser and lifelong hunter. “We just want our state government and our state tourism industry to understand the importance of in-state hunters. I think there’s a real strong feeling that we’re being taken for granted.”

Johnson, who lives in Watertown, recently wrote a column in the South Dakota Searchlight that dug into this trend — and struck a nerve with locals. He acknowledges that nonresidents are the “financial backbone” of the state’s pheasant program, thanks to higher license fees. (Residents pay $36 for a season-long small game license and a $10 habitat stamp; nonresidents pay $142 to hunt birds for 10 days, plus a $25 habitat stamp.)

“We understand that [financial dynamic] as South Dakota hunters. But at the same time, we need to start putting more emphasis on growing in-state hunting,” says Johnson. “We put so much of our advertising effort in out-of-state markets that we know where most of the hunters come from. And we don’t do similar types of advertising geared toward local residents and trying to figure out programs that are going to build new hunters within the state.”

DIY public-land pheasant hunting, especially during poor bird years, isn’t for the faint of heart. I’ve had to work for my limits of wild roosters over the seasons, slogging miles through nasty weather, thick cover, cattail sloughs, and rolling hills. Last weekend I hiked 9 miles over public ground with my dog (who covered 15 on his own four legs) and two buddies to fill our three limits. It was one of the best days of pheasant hunting I can remember.

For hunters with more cash and less interest in (or the physical ability for) such a grind, South Dakota offers hundreds of private shooting preserves. These lodges cater to businessmen, casual hunters, and the wealthy — almost exclusively out-of-staters who fly into hubs like Pierre and Aberdeen to shoot high volume put-and-take birds. Business is booming.

In the last quarter century, the number of licensed pheasant preserves across the state has grown substantially, from 157 in 2001 to a record 237 last season. Preserves must be a minimum of 160 acres (and no more than 2,560 acres). And over the past nine seasons, the harvest of released captive pheasants shot on preserves has climbed 50 percent (this excludes incidental harvest of wild birds). During the 2025-26 season, hunters shot about 400,000 pheasants on preserves — a record high.

“Everybody’s got a story about why they don’t hunt now, and all other problems that they’ve had getting access compared to how it used to be,” Johnson says of local hunters. “There’s a shift in emphasis in South Dakota toward more the commercialization of hunting — and I get it. I’ve got a lot of friends who own hunting operations … They’ve got really nice hunting operations. They’re all paid hunting and geared almost 100 percent to out-of-state hunters … Very few people in South Dakota are going to pay for that type of experience.”

Residents simply can’t afford the rates — from $2,000 to $4,000 per day at the fanciest lodges, he says — that traveling hunters are willing to pay. Meanwhile, hunting operations are leasing private land for their clients. This is more of an issue in east-central South Dakota, in the heart of pheasant country.

This steady rise in preserve pheasant hunting also contributes to access fees or the leasing of private land that could otherwise be open for permission to residents. After doing some work for a real-estate client one year, Johnson asked if he could hunt their property.

“They said, ‘Well, is it pheasant hunting? And if it’s pheasant hunting, would you be willing to pay a little bit? If it’s duck hunting, just go ahead,’” says Johnson. “So we value our pheasants quite a bit.”

While the hunter numbers cited in this story focus on wild pheasant hunting, the data they’re drawn from is murky (more on this in a bit). SDGFP explicitly says “no shooting preserve license holders were surveyed and none of their harvest is included” in wild bird harvest estimates. But these annual figures undoubtedly capture some preserve hunts, since hunters can legally shoot pheasants on preserves using their small game licenses.

The state’s harvest reports also don’t include any details on where hunters are killing pheasants or if they’re paying for access.

One lifelong South Dakota hunter, who asked not to be named so as not to upset factions of the hunting community, still puts the permission success rate at about 50 percent near the Pierre area.

“When I was a kid, it was all wild birds. We’d hop on the tailgate, the kids would walk through the [nasty cover], and adults blocked or did the easy stuff. It was opening weekend and it was a tradition. I think that tradition is still there, and I think people want to celebrate it the same way, but it has been commercialized. It wasn’t commercialized when I was a kid. It was good old landowners who let people hunt.”

South Dakota’s most recent push to ramp up pheasant license sales began in 2020 with its “Hunt the Greatest” campaign. The collaboration between the state’s game and tourism agencies spent about $662,000 that year in advertising on cable TV, podcasts like MeatEater, and in paid searches online, among other avenues. (Outdoor Life has also received South Dakota tourism funding for sponsored campaigns.) And in 2024, the campaign targeted South Dakota plus 13 out-of-state markets, including Minnesota, Iowa, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Colorado, Texas, and Michigan.

Neither agency could provide the breakdown of spending by in-state and out-of-state dollars to OL by press time.

The Hunt the Greatest campaign launched the year following the state’s final roadside pheasant counts, in 2019.

“Then-Governor Kristi Noem did away with that [roadside brood count], and that was partly because of the pressure from the tourism industry,” says Johnson. Noem’s family owned a pheasant lodge, and she also described herself as an owner and operator of a hunting lodge. “If the report came out that bird numbers were down, that sometimes caused out-of-state hunters to not come.”

Concluding the best long-running and scientific data collection on the state’s bird numbers was controversial, to say the least. As one former pheasant research biologist with SDGFP put it, the state’s current hunter survey stats are “fake news” that are “not verifiable or scientific.”

“The loss of the brood survey … means we have no accurate information on South Dakota pheasant populations for seven years,” that biologist, Larry Fredrickson, wrote in a letter to the Huron Daily Plainsman this spring. “I hope the state gets the brood survey back soon … to get South Dakota pheasant management out of the dark ages.”

The harvest numbers Fredrickson refers to — which this story necessarily relies on, since it’s the only available data on recent pheasant hunting participation and harvest — elicit limited participation from residents (25 percent responded to the survey) and nonresidents (31 percent responded), among other issues.

Given that the state has discontinued those roadside brood counts, Johnson says South Dakota would rather nonresidents not know when it’s a bad pheasant year.

“Just believe us when we tell you, ‘Oh, pheasant hunting’s gonna be great,’” Johnson jokes. “But by doing that, we lose the scientific analysis on what really is happening with our bird population.”

It’s also unfair to traveling hunters, says 73-year-old resident duck and pheasant hunter Bruce Knowlan. No matter how much money they inject into the economy, most DIY pheasant hunters still have finite time and budgets to hunt birds.

“Hunting isn’t a sport anymore, it’s an industry,” says Knowlan of the canceled roadside counts and continued marketing during down bird years. “It’s crazy, it breaks my heart.”

None of the locals I spoke with for this story felt animosity toward well-mannered visiting hunters. That includes Knowlan, who lives in northeast South Dakota. The rural community he calls home is very welcoming to nonresident pheasant hunters.

“They like people who are spending money in the towns. They like nonresident money. They like their motels busy, they like their restaurants busy,” says Knowlan. “The only thing people around here hate is nonresidents coming into the area, buying farmland, and taking it out of [crop] production to put it into some program like CREP or CRP.”

In other words, farmers and residents are happy to have out-of-staters hunt pheasants, support local businesses, and maintain the area’s farming traditions and economy.

And indeed, nonresidents spent an estimated $161.8 million statewide during the 2025 season. While visiting hunters presumably spend more on expenses like lodging during pheasant season, it’s clear: resident pheasant hunters help drive the economy, too. Last year they spent an estimated $142.7 million in the state.

To Knowlan’s mind, there are fewer resident pheasant hunters in recent decades because there are simply fewer South Dakotans living in rural areas. Even as South Dakota’s population has grown steadily in the last few decades, most of that growth has gone into urban areas.

Case in point: The population of the northeast South Dakota county where Knowlan lives has steadily declined over the past century, dropping 64 percent to roughly 5,500 people in 2025. Meanwhile, farms have been consolidated, which means there are fewer landowners to ask for permission to hunt the same amount of ground.

“It’s fascinating to me that if you take the back roads from my place into town, there used to be a farm every 80 acres,” says Knowlan, adding that families used to have more kids, too. “I would go by a hundred kids’ homes in a six-mile radius. And now, on that same road, there’s maybe four. They’re bigger farms.”

Consolidation of small farms and the rise of hunting leases and access fees are key reasons Knowlan says it’s “much, much harder” to get permission on private land than it was decades ago.

“Residents aren’t going to go out and lease the neighbor’s land so they can go pheasant hunting,” says Knowlan. “It’s still a family tradition around here, but not like it used to be, where everybody would quit working at noon on Saturday and go pheasant hunting at the neighbor’s.”

Still, he doesn’t think South Dakota is different from any other state when it comes to diminished private access. Before he bought his South Dakota farm in 2011, Knowlan was a DIY hunter from Minnesota who hunted all over North America — including South Dakota — each season. He remembers what it was like to ask for permission, and what it’s like to grant it.

“I do think a lot of guys still would allow pheasant hunting, if they don’t have relatives or family members they’re saving it for,” says Knowlan. “It used to be, I’d say, 90 percent of people would let you hunt. Maybe now, around here, it’d be 50 percent. But I would hate to be a young man, 16 to 20 years old [again], and not have a lot of money and want to do it yourself all over the country. It would almost be impossible.”

Yes, there are more nonresident pheasant hunters than South Dakota pheasant hunters, and that means they’re killing more total pheasants. But locals are enjoying longer hunting seasons and they’re killing, on average, more birds per hunter than visitors more often than not in recent years.

Last season nonresidents, who are more likely to shell out for private access, killed an average of 9.3 pheasants. Residents killed an average of 10.2 birds during their season, and most probably didn’t pay for the privilege.

For an even greater edge, Johnson would like to expand the special three-day resident-only pheasant opener that falls on the weekend before nonresidents are allowed to hunt.

“People feel that expanding that might be helpful for giving in-state residents a little bit more of an advantage.”

Resident youth license sales are also on the rise in recent years. South Dakota already has strong opportunities for new hunters — adults and kids alike — to get into pheasant hunting.

Youth and mentored hunters “have a 9-day period to themselves for pheasant hunting” prior to the regular season opening,” according to SDGFP regs. “This is an opportunity for adults to take young hunters out to experience, first-hand, the joy of hunting as well as the responsibility.”

Still, there’s at least one complicating factor to recruiting younger hunters into the fold: You must be 16 to hunt alone in South Dakota. Adjusting this age restriction for qualified teens might be another way to encourage participation.

I learned of this requirement just a few weeks ago, after agreeing to take a local 15-year-old and his retriever pheasant hunting. I assumed they were still learning the ropes and needed guidance on strategy and an extra gun for the dog. This was true enough, but the reality was he needed me to legally chase pheasants. This South Dakota teenager (whose parents don’t hunt) needed an adult alongside him to shoot pheasants. The irony is that he drove himself to our meet up. You can start driving solo at 14 and a half in South Dakota.

South Dakota has some of the best public-land access around, especially compared to other historic pheasant states like Iowa and Nebraska. There are 1.6 million acres open to public hunting across South Dakota, according to SDGFP. And indeed, I have never once thought to ask strangers for pheasant hunting permission in seven years of bird hunting here, because of the abundance of uncrowded public land. The number of private acres enrolled in public-access programs has also grown over the last decade.

Still, Johnson would like to see South Dakota invest in drivable access to its public lands. (This echoes a larger national debate around what constitutes “access” to public lands.)

“South Dakota’s got a tremendous amount of public land. I think there are things that Game, Fish and Parks can do in managing that land that makes it easier, especially for older hunters, to get on it,” says Johnson. “We might have miles of public land in one tract and the parking lot is out by the road. And it’s fenced off. And so if you wanna get access deeper into the land, you’ve got to be in good physical shape to be able to walk deeper into it.”

SDGFP communications manager Nick Harrington says the agency absolutely cares about resident pheasant hunters and its goal is to recruit, retain, and reactivate as many pheasant hunters as possible. He’s attending a women’s learn-to-pheasant-hunt event Sunday, and also cited the grand opening of the agency’s expanded outdoor campus in Sioux Falls on Thursday.

“This expansion project is important as GFP will be able to offer more programs year-round,” reports KELO-AM, “which will include archery, game processing, and classes taking students on their hunting journey from the field to the table.”

I have volunteered as an instructor at a women’s learn-to-pheasant hunt weekend in South Dakota every August for the last four years. I’ve offered sessions on everything from shotgun basics to bird dog demos to finding promising public hunting spots. These programs, and my hunt with that local teen and other new pheasant hunters I’ve taken out, reminded me of what I’ve learned from years spent reporting on the national hunter recruitment problem. New adult hunters are usually recruited into the sport only after two to three years of continuous mentorship and support from dedicated existing hunters. Youth programs typically only succeed at recruiting kids who are already from hunting families.

The best way to keep family hunting traditions alive, in other words, is to take family hunting — again and again.

There is one simple correlation around pheasant hunting that’s difficult to ignore: Both resident and nonresident pheasant hunter numbers are linked to wild pheasant numbers. When harsh weather leads to low bird numbers, fewer hunters go pheasant hunting. When winter snowfall and spring rains are mild, bird numbers shoot up, and more hunters buy licenses. This is true in recent years, which have seen excellent bird harvests.

The most dedicated pheasant hunters will keep buying licenses every year, no matter how poor or good the hunting. It’s a tradition, and the best ones, including South Dakota pheasant hunting, will endure as long as there are places to hunt and people there who welcome hunters.

On my way out of my public spot near the hard-working combines, I waved to the young farmer still idling in the grain truck. He stepped out of the cab with a broad smile on his face and, dangling on the step, hollered over the rumble of harvesters.

“I can’t afford to repair your truck!” I shouted back.

He shook his head at that and, still grinning, waved me on.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8536. Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

Taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

The 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition plan includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram

Interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#8534. “We Used FFS and Were Targeting Big Bass.” Angler Breaks 76-Year-Old Smallmouth Bass Record

Published Nov 4, 2026 4:14 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

On the morning of October 30 Austin Schiefer and his fishing buddy Ted Johnson launched their bass boat into Green Bay, a huge Wisconsin portion of Lake Michigan. They started about 7:30 working a reef area in 18 feet of water about two miles from shore. Before long, they’d go on to break a 76-year-old fishing record.

“It was a spot we’d fished previously and caught nice smallmouths on,” Schiefer tells Outdoor Life. “We used forward-facing sonar and were targeting big bass.”

The morning started windy, ideal conditions for clear water bass on Green Bay. The duo was catching bass, but about mid-day the wind died and the water got calm.

“That’s not the best conditions for Green Bay,” says Schiefer, who works for UPS when he’s not producing his own line of soft plastic lures (Schief’s Custom Baits). “There were plenty of bass on the reef, but they were finicky and wouldn’t take the lures I was casting.”

Johnson, however, was catching bass using a different type of soft plastic. He suggested to Schiefer that he try one of the lures he was doing well with, and to go lighter with his tackle.

“The bite was light and deep, so I changed to the setup that Ted suggested,” says Schiefer, from Menasha, Wisconsin.

Schiefer changed over to a Deps Sakamata Shad Soft Jerkbait, which is a 5-inch lure, and the productive hue was “champagne-pepper.”

He threaded the lure onto a 3/32nd-ounce jighead and made a long cast with the lightest 7-foot spinning rod he owns. His reel was spooled with 8-pound test Power Pro braided line with a 10-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

“I wanted to make a long cast and sort of swim the lure back as it sank, a pendulum like retrieve,” says Schiefer. “We could see fish on bottom with sonar, but they’d rise up to take lures. Except they were refusing my lures just before they’d hit – until I cast that Deps Jerkbait.”

It was about 2 p.m. and as Schiefer’s lure sank he felt a hit. But the fish didn’t fight like a smallmouth. The battle wasn’t fast and furious and there were no jumps. Just a couple minutes of it taking drag, and rugged deep pulling and rolling – so much so that Schiefer thought perhaps he’d hooked a freshwater drum.

“But as I worked it to the surface I got a look at it in that clear water about 10 feet down, and I saw that it was a huge smallmouth,” he says. “I knew it was a monster, and when I got it to the boat Ted netted it.

“I got lucky, because the hook was bent when I took the lure out of its mouth.”

Schiefer had caught big smallmouths previously, but nothing over 7 pounds, so he knew his catch was important. They put the lunker bass in their boat livewell and tried to contact Wisconsin’s Department of Natural Resources. But it was Friday afternoon before Halloween, and no one from the DNR was available.

The anglers quit fishing and trailered their boat to a grocery store where the bass was weighed at 9 pounds, 11ounces on certified scales. It measured 23.75 inches long. The smallmouth easily topped the 1950 Wisconsin record smallie weighing 9 pounds, 1 ounce. That fish was caught by Leon Stefonek in Oneida County’s Indian Lake.

To qualify as a state record bass, the DNR required the fish to be weighed and examined by state biologists. That didn’t happen until the next day, when DNR fisheries staff weighed and inspected the fish.

They discovered the bass was a male, not a female – which usually are the larger of the two fish genders. Additionally, Schiefer’s 9.70-pound smallmouth had nothing in its stomach, again unusual as most bass in autumn are feeding heavily for the coming winter.

Schiefer will have a skin mount made of his smallmouth bass record, which he says has been officially recognized by DNR as Wisconsin’s heaviest bronzeback of all time. He’s also considering having replica mounts made of the fish.

Read Next: 7 Forward Facing Sonar Tips: Settings, Mounting, and Techniques Explained

“I think a replica mount of the bass would be nice for the National Freshwater Fishing Hall of Fame in their Hayward museum, and maybe one for Bass Pro Shops, too,” he says.

“My only regret in all of this is I didn’t release the fish alive. I couldn’t with the DNR requirements for weighing and inspecting the fish for the record… I’ve had some sleepless nights because of that. I did everything in my power to keep from killing that bass.”

#8532. Hike to the End of the World Begins

After a restful zero day in Santiago de Compostela, we set out on the Camino Finisterre toward what ancient pilgrims believed was the “end of the world.”

Our albergue stay last night turned out just fine. Despite a few online reviews mentioning sewer smells and bed bugs, our room was clean and bug-free (or so we thought at the time—more on that in the coming days!). The streets below echoed with late-night partygoers, but having logged 500 miles, we slept soundly. It was a crisp, 40°F morning as we packed up to begin the next leg of our journey.

At 8:00 AM, we wandered out past the majestic Santiago Cathedral as the city slowly woke up. Our first order of business was finding breakfast, which led us to a cozy café packed with locals.

I enjoyed two cafés con leche while Knockerz had tea served in a charming cast-iron teapot. The owner brought out complimentary pastries and cakes with our drinks, and the entire bill came to less than $8!

Once we left the city streets behind, we crossed a small river flowing past an old mill and entered a dense forest. The atmosphere shifted almost instantly. Compared to the crowded, touristy energy of the final 100 kilometers into Santiago, the trail to Finisterre felt quiet, authentic, and peaceful.

The trail soon began a gentle climb through a thick eucalyptus forest, where the crisp scent filled the air like a spa. At the crest of the hill, we spotted a small tour bus and about a dozen people gathered near a lookout.

As we chatted with them, we were surprised to discover they were the American tour group that had paid for the Botafumeiro swinging ceremony during yesterday’s mass!

We thanked them again for making that unforgettable experience possible.

Their guide pointed out that historically, this spot was the final point where pilgrims could look back and see the spires of the Santiago Cathedral. From here on, pilgrims turned their focus entirely toward the Atlantic coast.

Warmed up from the climb, we shed our outer layers and plunged back into an ancient, shaded woodland trail.

Emerging from the forest, we followed a paved country road that wound downhill toward the valley. We had already covered half our daily mileage in under two hours!

At the bottom of the hill lies Ponte Maceira (near Aguapesada), a picturesque medieval village built along the Tambre River. The star of the village is a stunning 200-foot-long Roman stone bridge featuring multiple arched spans over the rushing water.

Crossing the river brought us to the hardest challenge of the day: a steep, 700-foot elevation gain over just half a mile. We paced ourselves and made it to the top without much trouble. From there, the trail wound through quiet countryside hamlets along traffic-free paved roads, offering a very chill, laid-back vibe.

Before long, we strolled into Negreira and located our apartment in the center of town. Having an in-unit washer/dryer and an induction stove felt like luxury! We threw in a load of laundry and headed out to run a few errands.

After exploring town to find compression socks for Knockerz’s shin splints, we stopped by a small grocery store for supplies. We spent the evening cooking a homemade meal, finishing our trail chores, and relaxing. Our first day on the Camino Finisterre was wonderfully low-key—a refreshing change of pace after the busy finish in Santiago.

#8530. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

In the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two plans. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later said it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

The Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

The 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

According to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt said that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

Mazeaud’s radio message said that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later said weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

Haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He said that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt said the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

The problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original plan of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth said the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#8529. These Are the 13 Tactics Expert Whitetail Hunters Actually Use to Tag Mature Bucks

Published Nov 4, 2026 5:13 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The best deer hunters in the nation (known and unknown) all share a common thread. They are students of deer and the woods, and they never stop learning. As such, they continually experiment with new and advanced deer hunting tactics.

In order to learn some of these secrets (and to share them with you), I called a handful of the best deer hunters I know. Here’s how they find success season after season.

Mark Drury of Drury Outdoors has bagged more big deer than most. His approach is proven, and the process he uses includes saving and analyzing a lot of trail camera data, especially historical information. He has kept every single trail cam pic of a racked buck since 2007.

“Save trail monitoring pictures in an organized fashion for easy review in future years,” Drury says. “Bucks are incredibly habitual from year to year. Study your pics year-round to formulate patterns with individual bucks or areas. [Over time you’ll build] a database that helps lead to patterns in future years, as crop rotations, weather, and moon in future seasons mirror conditions that occurred in the past. It takes a lot of time to assemble and study but saves time in future seasons.”

Grant Woods of Growing Deer TV is one of the most renowned deer scientists in the country. He seems to get inside the mind of whitetails and understands what they do and why they do it. To that point, he stresses making hunting decisions based on what deer do, and not what we think they should do.

“An issue I’ve seen is hunters making setup and tactical decisions based on human thoughts,” Woods says. “The hunters I know that have repeated success filling tags in all types of conditions and habitats always think like a deer. They consider what deer need that day, and what will deer avoid.”

As Paul Beasley, co-host of “Canada in the Rough” TV, says, hunters are creatures of habit. “The longer we hunt a piece of ground, the more established our hunting setups and entry/access/travel points become,” he says. “We tend to rely more on what has worked before, and while deer in general also tend to gravitate to the same trails, food sources, and pinch points, it has been my experience that mature bucks need to be treated as individuals and hunted accordingly.

“The buck I shot this year helps illustrate my point. We have hunted this same 100-acre property for over 10 years, and have always taken deer off of it in the same 50-yard-by-80-yard area. Throughout the spring and into summer, this buck was working that area perfectly, but as hunting season approached, his behavior changed. His appearances on camera began to fall off. So, I scrambled to put up more cameras and found that he hadn’t gone anywhere. He was just using different parts of the property.”

Beasley killed that buck on the second afternoon of the season. He arrowed from a setup that his crew had never harvested a buck from before.

“It was through paying attention to this individual buck’s behavior, and not just doing the same old thing that has always worked, that allowed me to put my tag on him,” Beasley says.

Oftentimes deer hunters do things without thinking. We react, rather than making decisions based on logic. HeadHunters TV’s Nate Hosie agrees, and says we should hunt smarter and not harder.

“Growing up, I used to think the more I was out there the better my chances,” he says. “It’s not completely wrong, but as I’ve grown as a hunter, I’ve learned to pick my moments for when to strike. Wind, temperature, time of year, trail cam intel, [and more] now go into my hunt. The less I’m in and out, and the higher probability my attempts are, the more success I find.”

Rick White is a longtime staple in the outdoor industry and he suggests that hunters go all or nothing with scent management.

“One of the biggest things I try to instill in people is always going to the woods as scent-free as possible,” he says. “Always play the wind. Never intentionally hunt a stand on a bad wind. But also know that deer don’t always come in from where we want them to. So, if you’re not going to follow every step with scent elimination, then save your money.”

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work

It sounds like rudimentary advice, but even experienced hunters make blunders that lead to being seen, heard, and smelled by deer. It’s something we must continually keep at the forefront of our mind. Will this entry route cause bedded deer to see me? Will this exit route blow scent into a bedding area?

Bone Collector Co-Host Nick Mundt knows deer hunting as well as anyone. As a former deer hunting guide and current big deer killer, he stresses the importance of going undetected when getting in and out of your hunting spots.

“Never think the wind will just work,” he says. “Always know that they’ll bust you if the wind is wrong. It dictates every sit.”

Aaron Gaines of Ani-Logics advises hunters to kill a target buck as early as possible. The early season and pre-rut offer opportunities to hunt consistent bucks.

“This is when he’s on a pattern and most predictable,” Gaines says. “To do this, I utilize most recent information from cameras. I’m very disciplined on hunting the right wind. If he’s daylighting, and I’ve got the right wind, things usually work out well.”

Read Next: Why the Last Week of October Is the Best Time to Kill a Big Buck

During the rut, whitetail bucks seem to travel via loops. That’s not hearsay or some hokey hack from your grandaddy’s hunting journal. That’s straight from a deer biologist. More specifically, former CEO of the Quality Deer Management Association and current HuntStand biologist, Brian Murphy.

“The biggest piece of advice I’ve learned over the years is to develop a plan and then stick with it long enough for it to have a reasonable chance of success,” Murphy says. “In other words, informed optimism. The hunters who have done their homework and keep a positive attitude, often after multiple dismal outings, are ultimately the most successful. Knowing from research that bucks often take a few days to complete loops within their home range, it’s not surprising that it takes persistence to increase the odds you will get an opportunity.”

Nathan Mrnak, COO of Base Camp Leasing, is a diehard deer hunter. He spends many days in the field each year. He stresses that it’s OK to move off your original plan and make a move.

“Picking out a stand location can be one of the toughest decisions while setting up on a mature whitetail,” he says. “I have had many first sits that ended with my target buck just out of bow range. Seeing his exact route provided the last bit of intel to moving a set just 50 yards to capitalize the next sit. This has worked time and time again in big timber.”

The most basic element of deer hunting is hunting deer where they are. To do that, you need current information.

Own the Season’s Art Helin knows this well. “Hunt where the bucks want to be during the correct phase of the season,” he says. “Food sources during early season, transition areas during the pre-rut (between field and bedding and staging areas), funnels and ridge edges during the rut (all day or mid-day sits especially), and back to food sources late season.”

During the rut, a lot of deer hunters choose to do all-day sits. Whitetail Properties Land Specialist Ben Harshyne does, too. However, he changes things up.

“I grew up hunting all-day sits in one stand,” he says. “Over time, I learned that deep timber and thick cover are action-packed in the morning and afternoon, yet often go cold by evening. In the afternoon, shift focus to hunting cover and edges near food sources or along travel lines leading to food. Not necessarily the actual food edge, but nearby. Does bed near food and still want to feed — and the bucks know it. Few stands are productive all day, so fine-tune your late-day move to target cover that relates to food.”

Big buck killer Jared Mills has arrowed a lot of big whitetails. He says don’t be afraid to be aggressive, but do it at the right time.

“I think most guys tend to be too conservative when hunting a target buck, staying on the fringes and only getting out when the conditions are perfect,” he says. “That’s fine if you have the entire season to hunt, and there’s little chance of him getting killed by a neighbor, but that’s a very rare scenario for most of us. While the windows of opportunity to encounter a target buck are already small enough, we make them even smaller by not getting in there after him. Be smart with your hunting, of course, but don’t sit around waiting for the absolute perfect time to move in, otherwise, you’ll likely miss a chance.”

Finally, just keep hunting. You won’t always kill a deer on opening day. It might just be closing day. So, keep hunting, and don’t give up.

“Have patience and persistence,” Helin concluded. “The entire season can change, and it can all happen in a short minute. Stay with it, and never give up, but also never get lazy. Always follow the same regimen from day No. 1 until the end.”
